opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. When I look back over the last twelve years, a few moments really stand out, and a lot of them connect to the thread of reinforcement learning combined with deep learning.

The first one for me is DQN, the Atari work. That was the moment we showed that a single agent, learning from pixels and a reward signal, could reach human-level play across dozens of different games without being told anything game-specific. Before that, deep learning and reinforcement learning felt like two separate communities. DQN showed that you could put them together and get something general.

Then AlphaGo, which was a cultural moment as much as a technical one. Go had been seen as a grand challenge for decades, and people thought it was maybe ten years away. Beating Lee Sedol, and especially seeing moves like move 37, showed that these systems could do more than imitate humans. They could find genuinely new ideas. AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero then took the human data away entirely and showed that self-play alone could get you superhuman performance across Go, chess and shogi. MuZero pushed that further by learning the model of the environment itself, so you didn't even need to be given the rules.

Outside of games, AlphaFold is probably the clearest example of AI delivering real scientific value. Protein structure prediction was a fifty-year-old problem, and seeing it essentially solved changed how biologists work.

And of course the other huge arc is the transformer and the scaling of large language models: GPT-3, and then ChatGPT, which made it obvious to everyone that these systems were useful in everyday life. What I find most exciting now is that the two threads are coming back together. We have these very capable pretrained models, and reinforcement learning is how you get them to reason, plan, and act as agents. A lot of the lessons from AlphaGo, like search, self-play, and learning from your own experience, are becoming central again in the language model world. So in a way, the milestones of the last decade are converging.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I look back over the last twelve years, a few moments really stand out to me, partly because I was lucky enough to be close to some of them.

The first is the DQN work on Atari, around 2013 and 2014. Before that, deep learning and reinforcement learning were mostly separate worlds, and people were skeptical you could combine them stably. Showing that a single network could learn to play dozens of games directly from pixels, with the same algorithm and the same hyperparameters, was a proof of concept that end-to-end learning of control was possible. Techniques like experience replay and the target network sound simple now, but they unlocked a whole research program.

The second is AlphaGo in 2016, and then AlphaGo Zero and AlphaZero. Go was considered a decade away. Beating Lee Sedol mattered culturally, but for me the deeper milestone was AlphaGo Zero, where we removed human data entirely and the system learned purely from self-play. It showed that search plus learning, combined with a well-designed self-improvement loop, could surpass the accumulated knowledge of centuries. And AlphaZero generalising to chess and shogi with no domain changes was the point where it felt like a general method rather than a trick.

The third is the transformer and the scaling era. Attention Is All You Need in 2017, then GPT-2, GPT-3, and the scaling laws work showed that predictable improvements came from scale and data in a way nobody had fully internalised. That changed how the field allocates effort.

Then I'd point to AlphaFold 2 in 2020. It was the clearest demonstration that these methods could solve a real, long-standing scientific problem, not just a game. For many of us that was validation of what we had hoped the work on games would lead to.

And finally, the last few years, where reinforcement learning has come back into the centre through RLHF and now reasoning models trained with RL on verifiable tasks. In a sense the two threads I've spent my career on, deep RL and large-scale learning, have merged. The ideas from AlphaGo about spending compute at inference time, searching and verifying, are now appearing in language models. That convergence is, to me, the defining story of the period.

astra-6.text:
For me, a few milestones stand out. One is AlexNet, which showed how powerful deep learning could be when you combine neural networks with enough data and compute. That really changed the direction of the field.

Then there was deep reinforcement learning—first learning to play Atari games from pixels, and then AlphaGo. AlphaGo was particularly striking because Go had seemed so far beyond what our existing approaches could handle. And with AlphaZero, we saw how much could emerge from learning through self-play, rather than relying on examples of human play.

I would also highlight the Transformer and the rise of large language models. That brought us toward systems that can perform a wide range of tasks through the same interface. ChatGPT made that progress tangible to people outside research: suddenly, anyone could have a conversation with an AI and discover what it could do.

What connects those milestones, to me, is learning. We’ve repeatedly found that systems can learn capabilities that would be extraordinarily difficult to program explicitly.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d probably highlight three. The first is deep learning really starting to work at scale—showing that we could learn useful representations from data rather than having to engineer everything by hand.

The second, for me personally, is AlphaGo. It brought together deep learning, reinforcement learning, and search to solve a problem that had seemed incredibly difficult. And then AlphaZero took that further: starting from the rules and learning through self-play, rather than relying on examples of human play. That was a powerful demonstration of what learning from experience could achieve.

The third is the emergence of large language models. We went from systems that were very capable within a narrow domain to systems that could do useful things across a huge range of tasks, through the same interface. What I find particularly exciting is how those threads might come together—broad knowledge from language models, combined with the ability to reason, search, and learn from interacting with the world.
